title: How do strong schools stay strong?
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison, a senior leader at Durrington, reports on his leadership team's discussion of the SSAT paper 'How do strong schools stay strong - 2026 Edition', written by Alex Galvin. He summarises its central message that lasting success comes from protecting what works and holding consistently high expectations rather than adding initiatives. His seven-point summary covers keeping the main thing the main thing, combining consistency with a healthy dissatisfaction, developing people, building organisational depth, attending to cultural detail, staying outward-facing and letting purpose beat accountability. He then lists eight questions James Crane drew from the report for the leadership team, ranging from initiative creep and teacher improvement to pupils who feel unknown and what the school would do if it ignored Ofsted. Allison says the team will not turn the report into another action plan but will use it as a test of organisational maturity, with extra attention on succession, the impact of professional learning and uneven pupil experience.
points: Strong schools sustain success by doing ordinary things extraordinarily well and filtering out noise rather than introducing new initiatives.
The paradox of strong schools is to be stable without becoming static, keeping a healthy dissatisfaction that spots marginal losses early.
Culture lives in the details of behaviour, adult language, routines and follow-up, so tolerating small slippages lets strong schools erode.
Resilient schools build depth through succession planning and middle leadership instead of depending on particular individuals.
The best schools decide from their values and pupils' needs, and leaders should test themselves with questions on variation, impact and pupils who feel unknown.
quotes: Its central message is that sustaining success is not about constantly introducing new initiatives, but about protecting what works, maintaining consistently high expectations and continuing to improve without becoming complacent.

Strong schools don’t depend excessively upon particular individuals. They develop future leaders, talent-spot, provide leadership opportunities, plan succession and assume that people moving into promoted positions require development and coaching.
Consistency of behaviour, adult language, follow-up, routines, relationships and expectations collectively sustains culture.

The best schools make decisions from their values and what pupils need rather than continually asking what Ofsted wants. Accountability matters, but it shouldn’t become the organising principle of school improvement.
Is every teacher genuinely better than they were this time last year, and what evidence would allow us to answer that confidently?
Which pupils attend, behave and achieve reasonably well but still don’t feel genuinely known, valued or connected to the school?
We’re not planning to use this report to generate another action plan. I think that would actually miss its message.
